title: Many Judaisms
hookLine: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argue over law and Temple

lines: A YOUNG MAN TRIES ALL THREE.
cards: One man in Jerusalem wants to find the right way to live, so he tries all of them. That's how the historian Josephus describes his youth.
There were, he says, three schools of thought among the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. He went through all three, from the inside.

Then, still not satisfied, he went out to the desert to live with a teacher named Bannus, who wore clothes made from what grew on trees, ate only what grew wild, and bathed in cold water day and night.
Only after that did he come back to the city and choose. In those days, being Jewish came in more than one shape.

teach.b: Here's how Josephus lays out the schools. The Pharisees keep many customs handed down from the fathers that aren't written in the law of Moses, and teach that souls live on after death.
The Sadducees hold that only the written laws are binding, and say the soul does not outlive the body; Josephus says they were fewer but included people of high rank.
The Essenes live in close communities and share their property, so that no one among them is rich and no one is poor.
And Josephus adds a fourth group, followers of Judas the Galilean, who say God alone is their ruler and will call no man master. The Mishnah lets us hear two of these groups argue.
In tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees complain to the Pharisees: you say holy scriptures make the hands impure, but the books the Mishnah calls Hamiram don't? Some readers take that word to mean Homer.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai answers, and the debate goes on, round after round. Notice the shape. These aren't people who've lost their faith.
They care so much about the Torah and the Temple that they argue about every detail: what counts as Torah, who should run the Temple, what happens after death, how to live.
There were many ways to be Jewish, and the Mishnah keeps the Sadducees' complaint in their own words.

how: Jews today belong to different movements and communities, such as Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others, and study the Second Temple sects through the Mishnah, the Talmud and the writings of Josephus.

o: several Jewish groups at once, arguing over Torah and Temple
Jews scattered abroad, each speaking another language
a split that made the Sadducees a separate religion

p: customs handed down from the fathers

s: in those days there was only one way to be Jewish
Josephus describes Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and a fourth group, and the Mishnah records arguments between them.
the Mishnah records Sadducees and Pharisees arguing with each other
in tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees say: we complain against you, Pharisees.

so that, he says, no one among them was rich and no one poor.

games.q: you're young Josephus in Jerusalem, wanting to find the right way to live. there are three schools. what do you do?
o: pick the biggest one and stop asking.
go through all three, then live with a teacher in the desert.
decide none of them matter and walk away.
games.why: Josephus says he went through all three schools, then lived with Bannus in the desert, and only then came back to the city and chose.

practice: Bring to mind a group whose way differs from yours, another congregation, another party, a family down the street that keeps its customs differently or keeps none, and picture one actual person from it, with a face and a name.
Ask what they care about enough to argue for, and find one thing you can honestly respect, without having to agree. If you pray, use words from your tradition to wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Many Judaisms. Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others, all arguing over Torah and Temple in the same land at the same time. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Perushim, the Mishnah's name for the Pharisees, as in tractate Yadayim.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways then too. They argued because they cared so much. See you tomorrow.
